name: White Stock (Fond Blanc)
description: A clear, neutral stock made from un-roasted bones. The backbone of light soups, velouté sauces and braises.
method: Blanch the bones: cover with cold water, bring to a boil, drain and rinse to remove impurities.
Return bones to a clean pot, cover with 4 litres cold water and bring slowly to a bare simmer.
Skim the surface continuously to keep the stock clear; never let it boil hard.
Add the vegetables and bouquet garni after the first hour of simmering.
Simmer gently 4–6 hours (chicken) or 6–8 hours (veal), skimming as needed.
Strain through a fine sieve or muslin, cool quickly, and refrigerate. Remove set fat before use.
technique_notes: Cold-water start and gentle simmering are essential for clarity. Boiling emulsifies fat and clouds the stock.

name: Brown Stock (Fond Brun)
description: A deep, savoury stock made from roasted bones and vegetables. The base of espagnole, demi-glace and rich gravies.
method: Roast the bones in a hot oven (220°C/425°F) until deep brown, about 45 minutes.
Add roughly chopped vegetables and tomato paste; roast 15 minutes more for colour and depth.
Transfer everything to a stockpot. Deglaze the roasting tray with water and add the scrapings.
Cover with cold water, bring to a gentle simmer and skim.
Add the bouquet garni and simmer 6–8 hours, skimming regularly.
Strain, cool quickly and chill. The Maillard browning gives colour and roasted aroma compounds.
technique_notes: Roasting develops Maillard reaction products — pyrazines and melanoidins — for caramel and roasted aromas.

name: Fish Fumet
description: A quick, delicate stock from white fish bones, used for seafood sauces and risottos.
ingredients: 1 kg white fish bones and heads (gills removed)
method: Rinse the bones well in cold water to remove blood.
Sweat the vegetables gently in a little butter without colouring.
Add the bones and sweat a few minutes more.
Add the white wine and reduce by half.
Cover with cold water, bring to a bare simmer and skim.
Simmer only 20–30 minutes — longer makes it bitter. Strain gently without pressing.
technique_notes: Fish fumet must be cooked briefly; over-extraction releases bitter compounds from the bones.

name: Dashi (Japanese Stock)
description: The umami foundation of Japanese cuisine, made from kombu seaweed and bonito flakes. Rich in glutamates and inosinates.
method: Wipe the kombu and soak it in the cold water for 30 minutes (or several hours for cold-brew).
Heat slowly and remove the kombu just before the water boils to avoid sliminess and bitterness.
Bring to a brief boil, then add the bonito flakes and immediately turn off the heat.
Let the flakes steep 1–2 minutes, then strain through muslin without pressing.
The result (ichiban dashi) is the prized first stock; the spent ingredients make a second, milder dashi.
technique_notes: Kombu provides glutamate and bonito provides inosinate — together they create a powerful umami synergy.

name: Vegetable Stock
description: A clean, aromatic plant-based stock for soups, risottos and vegetarian sauces.
method: Roughly chop all vegetables to expose maximum surface area.
Optionally sweat them in a little oil for a sweeter, rounder flavour.
Cover with cold water, add aromatics and bring to a gentle simmer.
Simmer 45 minutes — vegetables give up their flavour quickly and turn bitter if overcooked.
Strain and use, or reduce for a more concentrated base.
technique_notes: Avoid brassicas (cabbage, broccoli) and starchy potatoes which cloud and sour the stock.

name: Roux
description: Equal parts fat and flour cooked together — the thickening base for the classic mother sauces and gumbos.
method: Melt the butter over medium heat until foaming.
Whisk in the flour to form a smooth paste.
Cook to the desired colour: white roux (2 min, for béchamel), blond roux (5 min, for velouté), or brown roux (15+ min, for espagnole and gumbo).
Cook out the raw-flour taste before adding liquid.
Add liquid gradually off the heat, whisking to prevent lumps, then return to the heat to thicken.
technique_notes: The darker the roux, the more flavour and the less thickening power, as toasting breaks down starch.

name: Béchamel (White Mother Sauce)
description: Milk thickened with a white roux — the base for Mornay, soubise, cream and cheese sauces.
ingredients: 1 onion piqué (studded with clove and bay)
method: Make a white roux with the butter and flour, cooking 2 minutes without colour.
Gradually whisk in the warm milk off the heat to keep it smooth.
Add the onion piqué and simmer gently 15–20 minutes, stirring, to cook out the flour.
Season with grated nutmeg, salt and white pepper.
Strain for a silky finish. For Mornay, whisk in grated Gruyère and Parmesan off the heat.
technique_notes: Warm milk and constant whisking prevent lumps. Nutmeg is the classic aromatic partner.

name: Velouté (Blond Mother Sauce)
description: A light stock-based sauce thickened with blond roux — base for suprême, allemande and white wine sauces.
ingredients: 500 ml white stock (chicken, veal or fish)
method: Make a blond roux, cooking the flour until lightly golden with a faint nutty aroma.
Gradually whisk in the warm white stock off the heat.
Simmer gently 20 minutes, skimming any impurities that rise to the surface.
Season and strain.
Enrich with a liaison of egg yolk and cream (for allemande) or with cream and reduction (for suprême).
technique_notes: The quality of the velouté depends entirely on the stock — it carries the sauce.

name: Espagnole & Demi-Glace (Brown Mother Sauce)
description: A rich brown sauce from brown stock and brown roux; reduced with more stock it becomes demi-glace.
method: Brown the mirepoix in fat until caramelised.
Stir in tomato paste and cook to deepen the colour (pinçage).
Add the brown roux, then gradually whisk in the brown stock.
Add the bouquet garni and simmer 1–2 hours, skimming constantly.
Strain. For demi-glace, combine equal parts espagnole and brown stock and reduce by half until glossy and coating.
technique_notes: Long, slow reduction and diligent skimming give demi-glace its deep colour and silky body.

name: Hollandaise (Emulsified Mother Sauce)
description: A warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter sharpened with acid — base for béarnaise, maltaise and mousseline.
method: Whisk the yolks and water in a bowl over a bain-marie (gently simmering water).
Whisk vigorously until pale, thick and ribbon-like (sabayon stage), keeping the heat gentle to avoid scrambling.
Off the heat, slowly drizzle in the warm clarified butter while whisking to build the emulsion.
Loosen with lemon juice and season with salt and a pinch of cayenne.
Hold warm (not hot). For béarnaise, replace lemon with a tarragon-shallot-vinegar reduction.
technique_notes: Temperature control is everything: too hot scrambles the yolks, too cold breaks the emulsion.

name: Tomato Sauce (Mother Sauce)
description: The classical tomato-based mother sauce; the foundation of countless Italian and Provençal dishes.
method: Sweat finely diced onion, carrot and garlic in olive oil until soft and sweet.
Add the tomatoes, crushing them, with basil and bay.
Simmer gently 30–45 minutes until thickened and the raw edge has cooked off.
Season with salt and a pinch of sugar to balance acidity.
Pass through a food mill for a smooth sauce, or leave rustic.
technique_notes: Slow cooking concentrates glutamates and develops the sweet, jammy depth of cooked tomato.

name: Mayonnaise
description: A cold, stable emulsion of egg yolk and oil — base for aïoli, rémoulade, tartare and countless dressings.
method: Whisk the yolks with mustard and a pinch of salt until smooth (all at room temperature).
Add the oil drop by drop at first, whisking constantly to start the emulsion.
Once thickened, add the oil in a slow steady stream.
Loosen with vinegar or lemon juice and adjust seasoning.
For aïoli, pound garlic into the base. If it splits, restart with a fresh yolk and whisk the broken sauce back in slowly.
technique_notes: Lecithin in the yolk binds water and oil. Add oil slowly and keep ingredients at one temperature.

name: Vinaigrette
description: The classic 3:1 oil-to-acid dressing — the most versatile cold sauce in the kitchen.
method: Combine the acid, mustard, shallot, salt and pepper and whisk to dissolve the salt.
Slowly whisk in the oil to form a light, temporary emulsion.
Taste and balance — add more oil if too sharp, more acid if flat.
Mustard helps hold the emulsion; whisk again before dressing.
technique_notes: Salt dissolves in the acid, not the oil — season the acid first.

name: Beurre Blanc
description: A warm butter emulsion built on an acidic shallot reduction — classic with fish and vegetables.
method: Simmer the shallots with wine and vinegar until reduced to about 2 tablespoons of syrupy liquid.
Reduce the heat to low.
Whisk in the cold butter a few cubes at a time, never letting it boil, to build a creamy emulsion (monter au beurre).
Season and strain if a smooth sauce is desired.
Hold at a warm, gentle temperature; it will break if overheated or chilled.
technique_notes: The emulsion relies on the milk solids in butter; keep the heat low and whisk constantly.

name: Fresh Egg Pasta Dough
description: The foundation of fresh Italian pasta — tagliatelle, ravioli, lasagne and more.
method: Mound the flour and make a well; crack in the eggs and add salt.
Beat the eggs with a fork, gradually drawing in flour until a shaggy dough forms.
Knead 8–10 minutes until smooth, elastic and silky.
Wrap and rest at least 30 minutes so the gluten relaxes.
Roll thinly with a machine or pin, then cut or shape as needed. Dust with semola to prevent sticking.
technique_notes: Kneading develops gluten for bite; resting makes the dough easier to roll thin.

name: Basic Lean Bread Dough
description: A simple flour-water-yeast-salt dough — the foundation of most everyday breads.
ingredients: 7 g instant yeast (or 100 g active sourdough starter)
method: Mix flour and water and rest 30 minutes (autolyse) to hydrate the flour.
Add salt and yeast and mix to a cohesive dough.
Develop the gluten by kneading or by a series of stretch-and-folds over the first hours of fermentation.
Bulk ferment until roughly doubled, 2–4 hours depending on temperature.
Shape, then proof until puffy.
Bake in a very hot oven (230–250°C) with steam for the first 15 minutes to set the crust and crumb.
technique_notes: Time and temperature drive fermentation flavour. Steam allows full oven-spring before the crust sets.

name: Neapolitan Pizza Dough
description: A long-fermented, high-extensibility dough for blistered, tender pizza bases.
method: Dissolve yeast in the water, add flour and mix to a rough dough; rest 20 minutes.
Add salt and knead until smooth and elastic.
Bulk ferment 2 hours at room temperature, then divide into balls.
Cold-ferment the dough balls 24–72 hours in the fridge for flavour and digestibility.
Bring to room temperature, stretch by hand (never roll), top sparingly, and bake as hot as possible.
technique_notes: Long cold fermentation builds complex flavour and a more digestible, extensible dough.

name: Shortcrust Pastry (Pâte Brisée)
description: A crisp, tender butter pastry for tarts, quiches and pies.
method: Rub the cold butter into the flour and salt until it resembles breadcrumbs (sablage).
Add the egg and just enough ice water to bring it together — do not overwork.
Form a disc, wrap and chill at least 30 minutes.
Roll out, line the tin, and chill again before baking.
Blind-bake with weights for a crisp base.
technique_notes: Keeping the butter cold and the handling minimal prevents gluten toughening for a short, tender crust.

name: Choux Pastry (Pâte à Choux)
description: A twice-cooked paste that puffs hollow — the base for éclairs, profiteroles, gougères and churros.
method: Bring water, milk, butter, salt and sugar to a boil.
Add all the flour at once and beat over heat until the paste forms a ball and films the pan (panade).
Cool slightly, then beat in the eggs one at a time until the paste is glossy and drops in a thick ribbon.
Pipe shapes onto a lined tray.
Bake hot (200°C) until puffed and deep golden; do not open the oven early or they collapse.
technique_notes: The water in the paste turns to steam and inflates the pastry; thorough drying keeps it crisp.

name: Pastry Cream (Crème Pâtissière)
description: A thick vanilla custard set with starch — the filling for tarts, éclairs and mille-feuille.
method: Infuse the milk with split vanilla and bring to a simmer.
Whisk the yolks, sugar and cornflour to a pale paste.
Temper by whisking in the hot milk gradually, then return to the pan.
Cook over medium heat, whisking constantly, until it thickens and boils for 1–2 minutes to cook the starch.
Off the heat, whisk in the butter. Cover with cling film on the surface and chill.
technique_notes: The starch protects the yolks from curdling, allowing the custard to be boiled to set fully.

name: Caramel
description: Sugar cooked to develop colour and flavour — the base for sauces, candies, and praline.
ingredients: optional: 100 ml cream + 30 g butter for caramel sauce
method: Wet method: dissolve sugar in water, then boil without stirring until amber.
Dry method: melt sugar gradually in a pan, stirring gently as it liquefies and colours.
Watch closely — caramel goes from amber to burnt in seconds.
Stop the cooking by adding warm cream and butter (stand back, it spatters) for a sauce, or pour out for brittle.
Caramelisation produces hundreds of new aroma compounds — buttery, nutty, bitter and fruity notes.
technique_notes: Do not stir a wet caramel before it colours or it can crystallise; brush down sugar crystals with water.

name: Mirepoix & Sofrito
description: The aromatic vegetable foundation of countless cuisines: onion, carrot and celery (French mirepoix) or onion, garlic, tomato and pepper (Spanish sofrito).
method: Dice the vegetables evenly — fine for quick dishes, larger for long braises.
Sweat slowly in fat over low-medium heat without colouring (mirepoix) for a sweet, mellow base.
For sofrito, cook longer until jammy and deeply caramelised, building rich savoury depth.
This aromatic base is the first layer of flavour for soups, stews, sauces and braises.
technique_notes: Low and slow sweating draws out natural sugars and builds a sweet foundation without bitterness.

name: Court-Bouillon
description: An aromatic acidulated poaching liquid for fish, shellfish and vegetables.
method: Combine all ingredients and bring to a simmer.
Simmer 20–30 minutes to extract the aromatics.
Strain, then use to gently poach fish or shellfish.
The acid firms delicate proteins and brightens the flavour.
technique_notes: Unlike stock, court-bouillon is built from aromatics and acid, not bones, and cooks quickly.

name: Clarified Butter & Ghee
description: Butter with the water and milk solids removed, giving a high smoke point and pure butter flavour.
method: Melt the butter slowly over low heat without stirring.
Skim the white foam (whey proteins) from the surface.
Pour off the clear golden fat, leaving the milky solids behind.
For ghee, continue cooking until the milk solids brown for a nutty, caramelised aroma, then strain.
Store at room temperature; it keeps far longer than fresh butter.
technique_notes: Removing milk solids raises the smoke point to ~250°C, ideal for high-heat cooking and emulsified sauces.

name: Knife Cuts (Brunoise, Julienne, Chiffonade)
description: Foundational knife cuts that determine cooking speed, texture and presentation.
method: Julienne: square off the vegetable, slice into thin planks, stack and cut into fine matchsticks (≈2 mm).
Brunoise: gather the julienne and cut crosswise into tiny, even dice (≈2 mm cubes).
Chiffonade: stack herb or leafy greens, roll tightly, and slice into fine ribbons.
Even cuts cook at the same rate and signal care and precision on the plate.
technique_notes: Uniformity is the goal — equal sizes cook evenly and look professional.

name: Brining & Curing
description: Salt-based techniques that season, tenderise and preserve proteins.
method: Wet brine: dissolve salt and sugar in water with aromatics; submerge the protein and refrigerate (1 hour per 500 g).
Dry brine: rub salt directly onto the surface and rest uncovered in the fridge for seasoning and crisp skin.
Brining lets proteins absorb water and salt, keeping them juicy through cooking.
Curing with higher salt concentrations and time draws out moisture for preservation (gravlax, bacon).
technique_notes: Salt denatures proteins so they retain more moisture and season throughout, not just on the surface.

name: Gastrique
description: A sweet-and-sour reduction of caramelised sugar and vinegar, used to balance rich and fruity sauces.
method: Caramelise the sugar to a light amber in a dry pan.
Carefully deglaze with the vinegar (it will spatter and seize, then dissolve).
Simmer until smooth and syrupy.
Add fruit juice or stock to build a sauce; the gastrique balances richness with bright acidity and caramel sweetness.
technique_notes: The caramel adds depth while the vinegar cuts richness — a classic sweet-sour-bitter balance.
